title: git add -A while subagents write to the tree commits their half-done files
symptom: A commit meant for one topic also contained intermediate `runs/*.out` files from another task, one of them cut off after two lines; subagents were still writing into that directory when the commit was made.
cause: `git add -A` stages the whole working tree, and parallel subagents write into the same tree; the parent session committed its own edits without checking what else was changing.
rule: While subagents are working in the tree, stage only your own paths (`git add <files>`); use `-A` only after their reports arrive. Tell a subagent that writes into the repo up front whether it commits its own folder or waits for the parent.

title: HubSpot preference pages embed every outcome; read only the visible text
symptom: Re-checking an address confirmation with curl: the URL path said `optin-confirmed`, the title said `Subscription confirmation`, but the page text contained `You have successfully unsubscribed from all email communications`. In a browser the same page shows only `Your email preferences were updated`.
cause: The HubSpot preferences-center template puts all possible outcomes into the HTML and hides the irrelevant ones with script and CSS. A side detail: the saved link contained a space, so curl refused it (`URL rejected`, exit code 000).
rule: Read the outcome of a confirmation page (HubSpot and similar) from `document.body.innerText` in a browser plus the URL path, with a screenshot; never conclude from the raw HTML. Strip whitespace from a link copied out of an email before passing it to curl.

title: A web form counts as submitted only when the site shows its confirmation text
symptom: Of six forms filled by script, three went through on the first try. A Gravity Forms form answered `Invalid selection` for every select field, but resubmitting on the response page worked. One form had a consent box that was a `div[role=checkbox]`, not an `input`. A hosted form (NoteForms) treated two fields as required although the markup had no `required`, and its multi-select picked the first option by itself when opened with the mouse. On another, focus left the first field twice. None of this is visible until you read the page after clicking.
cause: Forms validate their own component state, not the DOM: required-ness and selection live inside framework components. Pressing the button proves nothing.
rule: Proof of submission is the site's confirmation text (`Thank you...`, `We have received...`) on a screenshot. Order: dry run; check every field by its actual state (`aria-checked`, the text on a select button); screenshot; submit; read the page. For Gravity `Invalid selection`, set the selects again on the response page and resubmit. About 15 minutes later check the mailbox: some vendors do not store the data until the address is confirmed by email.

title: Gmail IMAP folder names are localized; a wrong name silently reads as empty
symptom: A test message was searched in `INBOX`, `[Gmail]/Spam` and `[Gmail]/All Mail`; the script printed `Spam: no, All Mail: no`, although the message was in All Mail.
cause: The mailbox has a Russian-language UI, so the folders are named `[Gmail]/Спам` and `[Gmail]/Вся почта`. Opening a non-existent folder failed, and the script swallowed the error and treated the folder as empty.
rule: Pick Gmail folders by `specialUse` flags (`\Junk`, `\All`) from `client.list()`, not by name; print a folder-open error instead of turning it into `not found`.

title: RLS probes with WHERE/RETURNING test the SELECT policy, not the write policy
symptom: After a 'verified' fix, an independent reviewer found within half an hour that a project member could rewrite `created_by` on someone else's task and delete it through an `author deletes` policy (or move it away by changing `project_id`). A second reviewer showed that the two main test probes and CI stayed green with the write policies reopened: four of nine single-policy regressions were not caught.
cause: `WITH CHECK` sees only the new row and cannot forbid changing an owner column; probes like `update ... where ... returning` and `insert ... returning` are stopped by the SELECT policy before the write policy is ever reached; the test was written against one known attack rather than against each policy.
rule: For an access-control fix: (1) owner columns are locked by column privileges or a trigger, not by a policy; (2) every write is probed twice, as the app sends it and bare (without `WHERE` and `RETURNING`); (3) one probe per policy; (4) acceptance is mutational: every single weakening of a policy or grant must turn CI red; (5) after each fix, a fresh independent break-it round on a live stand before publishing.

title: grant on all tables in schema opens tables the demo does not have
symptom: On a reviewer's advice the fix revoked and re-granted privileges `on all tables in schema public`. A second reviewer added a sixth table without policies; after those two lines any logged-in user could read and rewrite it.
cause: The demo has five tables, so 'all tables' equals 'our tables'; a reader's schema is different. One reviewer's advice was accepted without a probe on a neighbouring case.
rule: In code meant for publication name objects explicitly; test any 'all objects' command on a schema with one extra object. A reviewer's suggestion is a hypothesis like your own: counter-probe before applying.

title: Subagents share the session scratchpad and ask permission to delete their files
symptom: A second 'independent' reviewer worked in the same scratchpad folder as the first, where the first reviewer's files (including its patch) were lying; at the end it requested `rm -rf` of its own binaries, and the user saw and rejected the permission prompt.
cause: The task only forbade reading the repository; no draft directory was named and nothing was said about deletion.
rule: In a subagent task: give it its own directory (`/tmp/<role>-<round>/`), forbid reading other scratchpad directories, forbid deleting files. Before a repeat round, remove or rename the previous round's folders.

title: netsh portproxy and the firewall rule outlive Chrome; no UAC to relaunch
symptom: The handoff said 'one UAC prompt is the human step'; in practice the CDP port answered right after launching the Chrome launcher alone.
cause: `netsh portproxy` entries and the firewall rule survive Chrome closing; admin steps are needed only after a Windows reboot or a change of the WSL interface.
rule: First check (`netsh interface portproxy show all`, `Get-NetFirewallRule`) and run only the Chrome launcher script; run the full bring-up with UAC only if `curl http://<gateway>:<port>/json/version` does not return 200.

title: psql heredoc: a bare echo line swallows begin; the probe runs untransacted
symptom: A `truncate public.comments` probe inside a supposedly rolled-back transaction emptied the table in the test database: `ROLLBACK` answered `there is no transaction in progress`.
cause: A line `echo` (without the backslash) was concatenated with the following `begin;` into one invalid statement; psql without `ON_ERROR_STOP` kept going.
rule: Destructive probes only on a copy of the database and with `\set ON_ERROR_STOP on`; labels only via `\echo`; after `begin`, check `select pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned() is not null` or read the output before the probe.

title: An access-control fix needs probes for what must keep working
symptom: Two review rounds and a fact-check missed that after the fix the owner of a new project could not see their project or insert their first membership row (`insert ... returning` and the insert into `project_members` failed). Fresh reviewers found it by asking 'can the owner still...?', confirmed on PostgreSQL 16.14.
cause: The post-fix test repeated only the attacker's actions, all of which were supposed to fail and did. What was supposed to keep working was not tested; the fact-check compared the article with the scripts rather than the scripts with common sense.
rule: Any access-control fix gets two probe sets: what must stop working and what must keep working (create an object, add the first member, read your own rows); both in the test and in CI. Give an expert reviewer a temporary cluster and the task 'break the fix: a leak or a refusal of a normal action', not just the text.

title: Chrome reopened from the taskbar runs without --remote-debugging-port
symptom: The bridge was up and a tab was open; a minute later `/json/list` was unreachable: the user had closed the window and reopened the profile from the taskbar, so Chrome started with the same profile folder but without the debugging port.
cause: The taskbar icon launches Chrome with the profile command only, without the launcher's flags.
rule: Observe a human's actions in the project window without CDP, by window title (`Get-Process ... MainWindowTitle` via `powershell.exe`); the port returns only after a relaunch through the launcher, which kills the window, so do it only once the human is done. Clear a password placed in the clipboard as soon as the flow is cancelled.

title: Claude Code blocks foreground sleep; wait with a background until-loop
symptom: `sleep 150; ./res.sh` was rejected by the harness (`Blocked: sleep ... use Monitor`); a foreground wait with a 600 s timeout was moved to the background on its own.
cause: The harness forbids long foreground sleeps.
rule: Wait for a condition with `until <check>; do sleep 20; done` run in the background; for an event stream use Monitor (each stdout line becomes a notification, up to 30 minutes, then restart). Long jobs on the server still go through `setsid nohup`.

title: A server process tied to an ssh session dies with it; use setsid nohup
symptom: A local background task `ssh ... 'node script.js ... submit'` ended after about 40 minutes with no output, while the processes on the server kept waiting with stdout attached to the dead ssh channel: the first log line after the next event would have killed them with EPIPE.
cause: The server process's output was bound to an ssh session that dropped.
rule: Start long waits on the server as `setsid nohup node ... > ~/tmp/<name>.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &`, and poll the log from the laptop with short calls (a background loop or Monitor) that survive a disconnect.

title: Measure download speed per CDN and machine before saying 'cannot download'
symptom: From the laptop `files.pythonhosted.org` gave 24 KB/s (mirrors returned 403/404), `download.pytorch.org` 40 MB/s, Hugging Face 32 MB/s; from the VPS PyPI gave 20 MB/s, scp VPS to laptop about 3.5 MB/s, `apt` 0.6 MB/s.
cause: Different CDNs are throttled differently from this network; the earlier one-off measurement (HF about 3 KB/s) was not representative.
rule: Before concluding 'not downloadable', run `curl -w speed_download` per CDN from both machines; pull PyPI wheels on the VPS (`python3 -m pip download --only-binary=:all: --platform manylinux2014_x86_64 --python-version 3.12 ...`) and `scp` them over; take torch from `download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu`; for llama.cpp `git clone` from GitHub is fast while release archives are slow.

title: Hugging Face measured at ~3 KB/s from both machines (later a one-off)
symptom: A venv with torch installed in minutes, but a 548 MB model file reached only 200 MB after 25 minutes; `curl` measured 3026 B/s locally and 2593 B/s on the server.
cause: The channel to huggingface.co from this region looked narrow (and rate-limited without a token). Later the same day the measurement turned out to be a one-off: 20-32 MB/s from both machines.
rule: Do not plan downloads above 100 MB within a session; if a large model is needed, fetch it in advance through another channel (mirror, token, another machine).

title: An incognito-context tab always shows 'Log in'; check login on the default one
symptom: An alert said 'Chrome is not logged in'; the agent opened the monitor's search tab, saw `Log in / Sign up` and no avatar, and escalated to the user. The user opened the site in a new tab of the same Chrome: logged in.
cause: The monitor's search tab lives in an incognito context (logged-out polling by design), so its header always says Log in. The alert came from one failed page read in the logged-in context, possibly disturbed by unrelated probes in the same Chrome at that time.
rule: Check login state only on a page of the default context (`browser.defaultBrowserContext().newPage()` then open an account page and look for the avatar), never via the monitor's tab. Run one-off probes of other sites in a second Chrome and close your tabs afterwards (`window.open` of a foreign site spawns tabs unnoticed); do not call `bringToFront` in the working Chrome. Do not forward a single-read alert to a human without a second confirmation.

title: require('./x') resolves from the script's directory, fs paths from cwd
symptom: A one-off probe run as `cd ~/app && node /tmp/probe.js` failed with `Cannot find module './lib/sample'`, while files under `state/` were read fine.
cause: `require('./x')` is resolved relative to the file that calls it (`/tmp`), whereas `fs.readFileSync('state/...')` is relative to the current working directory.
rule: In one-off scripts outside the repo, require project modules by absolute path (`require('/abs/path/to/lib/sample')`); keep data paths relative to cwd or absolute as well.

title: Chrome drops session cookies on a clean start unless restore_on_startup=1
symptom: A vendor dashboard login made from the server's second Chrome worked one day; the next day the same profile opened the login page again, which was recorded as 'session expired' and led to a wrong conclusion that the dashboard needed another machine.
cause: The dashboard's only login cookie `session` is a session cookie (no expiry, httpOnly). On a clean start Chrome deletes session cookies unless the profile has 'Continue where you left off' (`session.restore_on_startup` = 1); the default is 'New tab' (5). Every visit that ended by stopping that Chrome would therefore begin with a fresh login.
rule: In the profile that holds dashboard logins set `session.restore_on_startup` = 1 (via `chrome.settingsPrivate.setPref` on `chrome://settings`, not by editing the file); after any new login, restart and verify the login is still alive. Before writing 'session expired', inspect the login cookie's expiry (`page.cookies()`: `session: true` means a session cookie).

title: pgrep -f and pkill -f match the shell that runs them; find processes by port
symptom: (a) One ssh command both launched a second Chrome and checked 'already running?' with `pgrep -f "chrome-form[s]"`: the check said yes, Chrome did not start, and the final `kill $(pgrep -f ...)` killed the shell itself (ssh exit 255). (b) `pgrep -f "ssh -i ... .*setsid nohup"` returned three PIDs, one of them the command itself (exit 144). (c) An hour later `pkill -f "chrome-form[s]"` sat in one command with a path containing the same word; the shell matched and died. Separately, `ssh 'cd ~ && DISPLAY=:99 setsid nohup google-chrome ... &'` never returned until the ssh was killed.
cause: `pgrep -f` compares the pattern with the full command line of every process, including the shell that invoked it. The bracket trick (`chrome-form[s]`) only avoids matching the pattern text itself; the same word elsewhere in the same command matches, and a regex with `.*` matches itself. ssh hung because `cd ~ && ... &` backgrounds the whole list in a subshell that keeps the ssh channels open until Chrome exits.
rule: Do not look for your own processes with `pgrep -f`/`pkill -f` at all: stop the second Chrome by the PID of the port listener (`pid=$(ss -tlnp "sport = :9223" | grep -o "pid=[0-9]*" | head -1 | cut -d= -f2); kill $pid`); find local processes by name (`ps -eo pid,comm,args | awk '$2=="ssh" && /.../'`). Background launch over ssh: `cd ~; <command> >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null & sleep 1; echo launched` (no `cd ~ &&` before the backgrounded command); check readiness in a separate call by `http_code`.

title: Two typing scripts in one browser: CDP keystrokes go to the active tab only
symptom: A form filled from the laptop's Chrome ended with the name field empty and `mail.com` in the email field while other fields were fine; a second script was exploring another form in the same browser with its own `bringToFront()`. A solo retry still lost the first field: typing started before the page gave focus. The submit was stopped both times by a value self-check before the click.
cause: CDP keyboard input goes to the active tab and active element; the second script switched tabs, and after page load the first click on the field did not focus it (a late page script).
rule: One typing script per browser at a time (never run exploration and filling in parallel, even in different tabs). Before typing, assert `document.activeElement === el`, otherwise click/focus again and retry; after typing, read the value back and compare; click submit only when every field matches.

title: SMTP `250 OK` means accepted by your relay, not delivered; check for a bounce
symptom: A submission was recorded as sent on the basis of `250 2.0.0 OK`. In the same minute a `Delivery Status Notification (Failure)` arrived: the recipient address was a Google Group closed to external senders. The inbox classifier filed the bounce as a foreign message and no alert was raised; it was found by eye in the log a session later.
cause: The address was taken from an FAQ where it was a form caption, not a mailbox. No post-send delivery check existed: `250 OK` means accepted by our SMTP server, not delivered. The classifier had no class for non-delivery reports.
rule: Count an email as delivered only after checking the mailbox for a bounce (about 15 minutes later; a `bounce` class now raises an alert). Take addresses from the contact/form page, not an FAQ. In the ledger call an unverified send 'accepted by SMTP', not 'submitted'.

title: An optional form step failed silently and left its modal over the submit button
symptom: The auto-submit got approval on two jobs and clicked submit three times on each; all six clicks ended in 'form reopened: not sent'. Screenshots showed a modal (`Add profile highlights`) sitting over the form with items already selected, present even before the first click.
cause: The site renamed the modal's confirm button (`Add N/4` became `Add to highlights`). The optional step looked for one label, got 'no Add button' and returned, leaving the window open. The form self-check did not look for modals, and the mouse click on the submit button hit the modal. An earlier lesson that labels are markup versions had been applied to the submit button but not to this step.
rule: An optional step that opens a window must return the page to its original state on any outcome: if it cannot confirm, close the window and continue without the add-on; an unclosed window is a self-check failure, not silence. Name the degradation in the send message. When one site label changes, grep every place that searches for that text, not only the one that broke. Fix proven by a dry run on the real form with the submit button's centre unobstructed.

title: Take click coordinates after scrolling; register a dialog handler first
symptom: Two hangs in one day. (1) Clicks on radio buttons and a text editor had no effect although `elementFromPoint` showed the right element. (2) After clicking Submit, every `page.evaluate` hung, then CDP dropped with `Network.enable timed out` and the tab had to be killed.
cause: (1) `scrollIntoView` ran inside the same `evaluate` that read `getBoundingClientRect`; the scroll happened, and for a tall element the top moved off-screen, so the click went nowhere. (2) The form shows a native `confirm('Are you sure...')`; without a dialog handler it blocks the renderer's main thread, so the page, not the script, hangs.
rule: Take click coordinates in a second call after scrolling and clamp vertically: `y = min(max(rect.y + h/2, 140), innerHeight - 140)`. Attach `page.on('dialog', d => d.accept())` before the first click on any submit button, and run the whole form pass as one script without pauses. Signature of this failure: `evaluate` hangs while `curl` to the site answers 200 within a second.

title: A site restores its autosaved draft asynchronously over freshly typed text
symptom: On a reply form the typed text was replaced a few seconds later by the previous version; three runs in a row would have sent the old text, and a title field was sent with the content doubled (`ParserParser ...`).
cause: The site saves a draft of the reply itself and restores it after page load, asynchronously and after the script had already cleared the editor and started typing. The title script also typed over a non-empty field.
rule: After navigation wait until the editor's content length stops changing (three identical readings), then clear and type. Before typing into any field, assert it is empty; after typing, compare the result with the source file character by character. If the site does not allow editing after submit, verification must happen before the click.

title: A wait loop built on pgrep -f matches its own command line and never ends
symptom: A background wait `while pgrep -f "node clientside.js"; do sleep 15; done` ran for 30 minutes although the measurement finished in 7. Repeated on 2026-09-23: a Monitor loop waited for `node autosend.js <id>` via `pgrep -f` inside its own ssh loop and would have lived until the timeout.
cause: `pgrep -f` searches full command lines, and the bash loop's own command line contains the same substring. The loop found itself.
rule: Wait by PID (`node x.js & pid=$!; while kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null; do sleep 15; done`) or by a result file. If pgrep is unavoidable, use a pattern that does not match its own text: `pgrep -f "[n]ode clientside.js"`. Before any `pgrep`/`pkill -f`, ask whether the string appears in the command you are running yourself.

title: A subagent that died on a network drop should be resumed by ID, not restarted
symptom: The user's internet dropped. A research subagent failed with `EAI_AGAIN` mid-work, while the pages it had already downloaded were lying in the scratchpad.
cause: The subagent calls the API from the laptop. The server and its daemons do not depend on the laptop's network, so nothing broke there.
rule: Continue a subagent that died on the network via `SendMessage` to its ID: its context is kept and the downloaded files are re-read from disk; a fresh launch repeats all the work. After a drop check three things: the server (units, locks, last poll), git (local equals origin), and unfinished background tasks.

title: Re-read shared state after any await; a stale copy overwrote another process
symptom: A record was marked `sent` by the auto-submit process, yet 90 minutes later its state card was back to `draft` without `sentAt`; a threshold counter saw 58 instead of 59. The card's `aliveCheckedAt` kept growing, which never happens for sent records.
cause: The listener's `sweep()` took cards from a snapshot, waited for the browser lock for one of them, then saved its whole copy. Meanwhile the auto-submit, holding the lock, wrote `sent`. The listener's pre-wait copy landed on top: a lost update between two processes. The card then lived as a draft until expiry, and the finalizer saw `sent` in the draft file and left the card alone.
rule: State written by several processes must be re-read from disk after any `await` that waits (lock, navigation, model call). Write into the fresh copy and only if the precondition (status) still holds. Regression: a stub wait function that writes 'as another process' during the wait.

title: A chat UI renders the message before the server answers; trust the response
symptom: A reply was typed and sent; the script checked that the text appeared in the thread and printed OK. Under the text stood `Couldn't send your message. Try again`, and `POST /inbox/conversations/messages` had returned 403. The client received nothing; it was caught by reading the output, not by the check.
cause: The frontend draws the message in the thread immediately, before the server replies. Failure is visible only as a separate retry element under the text. The check measured rendering, not delivery.
rule: Success of a send is only the server response: the POST returns 201 and no retry element is present. Text in the thread proves nothing. On a 403 do not press retry blindly: reload the thread, make sure the message is absent, and send again. General rule: a UI action is proven by the server response or the state after reload, not by what the frontend drew.

title: Fixtures from a read item miss the unread counter; dedup keys on volatile fields
symptom: The messages poller recorded the client's first message as `1` and put `room_xxx|1` into the dedup memory. The next single message from the same client would have produced the same `1` and been treated as already seen, with no reply and no alert.
cause: `parseRoom` took the preview as the last line of the card. The fixture had been captured from a room after the thread was opened, so it had no unread counter. The dedup key (room + preview) was built on a field that coincides across different events.
rule: Capture UI parse fixtures in both states: unread and read, before and after the action. Never build a dedup key on a field that can repeat across events (a counter, `Yesterday`, an empty preview). Verify the first live event of a new pipeline field by field against the source, not just by outcome.

title: A copied interactive CLI login expires; daemons need `claude setup-token`
symptom: For three hours every model call from the daemon answered `Failed to authenticate: OAuth session expired and could not be refreshed`; each job retried four times and sent a 'submit manually' message to the user.
cause: The CLI login on the server had been copied from the laptop. An interactive subscription login has a hard expiry stored in `~/.claude/.credentials.json` as `refreshTokenExpiresAt`; once past it, the first expired access token could not be refreshed and the CLI wiped both tokens. The expiry had been sitting in the file for 25 days unread. The pipeline also had no class for 'shared outage', so each job cycled through models. A long-lived token would not have worked either: the wrapper scrubbed `^CLAUDE` from the environment and would have dropped `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.
rule: Give daemons a login issued for the machine: `claude setup-token` (one year, scope `user:inference`) in `.env`, not a copy of an interactive login (shorter life, broader rights). When moving or issuing a credential, write down the day it dies and check environment filters on the call path. Treat a dependency shared by all models (login, the whole API) as its own error class: one message to the human with one action, hold the work and resume automatically. Capture error texts for regressions from the live CLI, not from imagination.

title: systemctl restart kills the whole cgroup, detached children included
symptom: The restart rule said 'between polls: last log line is `sleep NNNs` and the lock is free'. But the monitor spawns the drafter with `spawn(..., { detached: true })`, the drafter spawns the auto-submit the same way, and `systemctl show -p KillMode` is `control-group` for both units.
cause: Restarting a unit kills all processes of its cgroup, and `detached` does not help. The rule was written for the poll itself; after a poll the drafter lives 1-2 more minutes and the auto-submit with its verifier up to 5, mostly without holding the lock.
rule: Before `systemctl restart` of a long-lived daemon, its cgroup must be empty: `cat /sys/fs/cgroup$(systemctl show -p ControlGroup --value <unit>)/cgroup.procs` shows only `MainPID`. For the monitor additionally require the sleep between polls. Automation that restarts the daemon must check the same thing.

title: A nightly error summary must count only failures that were not healed by retries
symptom: The morning summary said 'errors in logs: 3 (3 kinds)': a `FAIL: RENDERER_STUCK` from both `monitor.out` and `runs.log`, and a `poll FAIL fetch failed`. The user forwarded them two nights in a row. Nothing was lost: the search was re-read by retry 13 s later and the poll succeeded 15 s later.
cause: `nightErrors` took every `FAIL` line. Both self-healing mechanisms log FAIL before retrying: true about the attempt, not the outcome. `monitor.out` is the stdout of the same `log()` that writes `runs.log`, so each monitor error appeared twice as two kinds.
rule: An alert to a human counts only what was not healed: for every retry mechanism the summary looks at the outcome (the next line of the same request) and lists healed failures separately with a count. When adding self-healing, teach the summary its outcome in the same change. Do not rewrite logs for the summary: logs are facts about attempts, interpretation belongs in the summary. Before aggregating several logs, check whether one is a copy of another.

title: An error that names its reset time is a wait state, not a terminal failure
symptom: Both models answered `You've hit your session limit · resets 4:10pm`; the pipeline handed the job to a human as failed and exited, 12 minutes before the reset, while the job's window still allowed 110 minutes.
cause: The wrapper only knew 'limit means next model', and at the end of the chain any error was terminal. The CLI states the reset time in the error, but the code did not read it; with a shared subscription limit there is no 'next model', and the only working move is to wait until the named moment.
rule: An error that names the moment the block lifts is neither a failure nor a decision: queue the job until that moment if it is before the deadline, and close with a fact if it is after. 'Submit manually' in unattended automation is a loss, not a safety net. Implemented as a `limitReset` parser plus `pending`/`retryAfter` state.

title: A fallback chain whose backup is the verifier turns review into self-review
symptom: The writer model hit its limit and the chain fell back to model B; the verifier was configured as model B too, so one model wrote and checked the same reply. Neither the log nor the human-facing message showed it, and the selftest was green.
cause: `fallbackModels` and `verifyModel` overlapped, and the rule 'writer differs from verifier' was checked only on the static config, i.e. the first pair. A fallback is a runtime state the config knows nothing about.
rule: For a writer plus verifier pipeline check all pairs of the Cartesian product of both chains: any intersection is a hole. A runtime collision must either pick a model from an independent line or raise a visible flag in the message and the ledger; never degrade silently to self-review.

title: Fallback between models sharing one subscription quota protects nothing
symptom: The config listed fallback chains like `[opus, haiku]` and `[sonnet, haiku]` as availability insurance.
cause: Only one model line had a separate limit counter; the other three shared the subscription quota. Confirmed on the server: one line returned 429 while the others still answered. A backup from the shared quota fails at exactly the same moment as the primary.
rule: Put fallbacks only between models with independent quotas. Within one quota a second model makes sense only as a different model for independent review, not as availability insurance; where nothing can insure, an empty chain and fail-closed (alert the human) is more honest than answering with an unmeasured model.

title: The subscription session limit is per account, not per machine or model
symptom: A test call from the laptop got `You've hit your session limit · resets 10:20pm` and the agent session broke for the second time that day; `claude auth status` on the server showed the same account, so any production call in that window would have hit the limit on every model of the chain.
cause: The session limit counts per account, not per machine or model; a per-model fallback chain protects against one model's limit, not the account's. A measurement run plus a long agent session exhausted the window in one evening.
rule: Run measurements in small portions, not while waiting for a client reply or with a draft in progress; search the server for the limit with the `(limit)` log marker across all logs. A separate account or API key for experiments is a decision for the owner if measurements become regular.

title: `claude -p --model <alias>` is resolved by the CLI version, silently
symptom: On the server (CLI 2.1.197) `--model opus` meant one model and an unknown alias meant the same model with no error, while a full model ID returned 400 `version 2.1.251 or newer is required`; on the laptop (2.1.263) the same aliases resolved to newer models. The log printed the requested alias, so the substitution was invisible.
cause: An alias is a convention of a specific CLI version; the wrapper returned `model: model || 'default'` (what was asked) instead of the `modelUsage` key from the JSON response (what was used). CLI versions on the two machines had not been compared for weeks.
rule: Put full model IDs in config; log the real model from `modelUsage`; after any CLI update run one alias-to-ID check via `modelUsage`; compare CLI versions on laptop and server at every sync.

title: 'Saved in the repo' needs git ls-files: .gitignore silently dropped the file
symptom: A commit message and the handoff said a measurement script was saved at `tools/.../probe-style.js`; the file was not in the repo (`git ls-files` empty, absent on the server) because a local `.gitignore` had `probe*.js` from the days of one-off probe scripts.
cause: The claim was written from the fact of writing to disk, not from the fact of landing in a commit; `git add -A` quietly skips ignored files.
rule: Confirm any 'saved in the repo' with `git ls-files <path>`; a file whose name matches an ignore mask needs an explicit `!name` in `.gitignore`.

title: A greedy gap in a verb...noun regex merges two matches; a negation kills both
symptom: `I would not book a meeting, but let's schedule a call on Monday` passed a stop rule even after switching to `matchAll`: `book\b[^.]{0,40}\b(call|meeting)` captured `book a meeting, but let's schedule a call` as one match, and the `not` before `book` cancelled everything.
cause: The gap `[^.]{0,40}` is greedy: it stretches to the last noun within 40 characters, so a second match cannot start inside it.
rule: In rules of the form 'verb ... noun' make the gap lazy (`{0,N}?`), iterate over all matches, and keep a 'refusal + promise in one sentence' case in the regression.

title: A test that greps the source for a call name pins the form, not the behaviour
symptom: After injecting I/O points into `handle()` for a behavioural run, a check failed because it searched the source for the string `verifyReply(cfg, ctx, out.reply`; the path worked, as a new behavioural run showed. The same check had never caught a real defect on that path.
cause: A source-text check verifies the call's name, not its result: a refactor breaks it for no benefit, and a real bug on the same path passes it.
rule: Regressions for pipeline scenarios are runs of the path with injected I/O points (thread, send, model, re-check; notifications and ledger through options), without a browser or a model; source-text checks only for what cannot be tested otherwise (a notification text, the presence of a command).

title: A test double without side effects hides state bugs in the mocked thread
symptom: An audit ran the reply engine with a stub where the sent message is appended to the thread as ours; a human's 'ok' after a hold then failed with 'thread changed since the decision': the key took the last message of the thread at all, while the pending key was built from the client's message. The existing regression (8 green checks) never saw it: its stubbed thread returned the same two messages whatever was sent.
cause: The stub modelled only the input (reading the thread) and not the consequence of its own output (what was sent becomes part of the thread); the human step lived in another process whose path was not stubbed at all.
rule: A test double must change state the way the world does: the sent text is appended to the thread as our message, and after each send the scenario runs the next human step on the same key. Compute idempotency keys and 'thread unchanged' from the last message of the counterpart, not the last message overall.

title: Button captions are a markup version; blur validation can race the form model
symptom: For an hour the auto-submit read a form as '4 required fields empty, no Send button', reloaded and refilled it 13 times, and closed the draft as expired. The screenshot at closing showed filled answers and a live green submit button with a new caption.
cause: The site shipped a new form: the button became `Submit proposal` without the number the code searched for. Also, answers filled programmatically (native setter + input/change + blur) showed `Value is required and can't be empty` on non-empty fields because validation on blur ran ahead of the form model; a second pass with the same values cleared the errors (4 to 0). Each reload did exactly one pass and reproduced the same errors.
rule: (1) Anything read by exact site text (caption, a number on it, an error phrase) is a markup version that changes without notice: match against a list of known captions and save evidence (screenshot plus the list of buttons and fields). (2) After programmatic fill, check validation errors next to each field, not just `value`; an error on a non-empty value means a second pass, not 'empty field'. (3) The same transient block after two or more identical refills is a code/site mismatch, not a page hiccup; tell the human what was searched and what is on screen.

title: Closing the last tab over CDP exits Chrome; hung embeds block load events
symptom: A script using `goto` with `waitUntil: domcontentloaded` (60 s) failed twice with `Navigation timeout` on the 6th-7th navigation of a series although the page was visibly rendered; `readyState` was `loading`/`interactive` and an embedded JSON blob was empty or truncated. Trying to revive the tab via `/json/close/<id>` closed the last window: Chrome exited and the CDP port went dead.
cause: The page keeps long-running loads (third-party iframes, trackers, a support widget): the load event does not fire while they hang, and after a series of searches they hang longer. A Chrome window with a single tab dies with it; CDP close does not distinguish a tab from the last tab.
rule: For a series of pages: `PUT /json/new?<url>` (new tab, no waiting), pause 10-15 s, close the previous tab, read the current one; parse embedded JSON only when `readyState === 'complete'`, otherwise wait and re-read. Never close a tab that is the last one in the profile; open the next one first. After any closes check the port with `curl -w '%{http_code}'`.

title: Clicks outside the viewport fail silently; tabs in a shared Chrome can vanish
symptom: `page.mouse.click` at the centre of a button's `boundingBox` 'worked' but no modal opened. Later the run died twice mid-way (`Target closed`, `Navigation timeout`); a `page.on('close')` watchdog confirmed the tab was closed from outside. Save had already gone through, so the edit was in place although the script ended with an error.
cause: (1) For an element below the fold `boundingBox` returns coordinates outside the viewport; a real mouse click lands outside the window without any error. (2) A one-off script's tab lives in the shared Chrome of the daemons: tab cleaners, memory discards and restarts promise it nothing, and 'run died' is not 'edit failed' (nor the reverse).
rule: Before a click, `scrollIntoView` and assert the point is inside the viewport (fail instead of clicking). Attach `page.on('close')` to the tab. Collect the proof of the result in a separate short read-only pass after the run, not as the tail of a long script. Before repeating a 'failed' edit, check the state of the world; every re-runnable edit script needs an idempotency guard.

title: Synthetic .click() is ignored by SPA modals; a field re-renders after Ctrl+A
symptom: `btn.click()` on an Edit button returned without error and no modal opened. After opening it with a real click, typing immediately after Ctrl+A left `F & Deploy...` in the field: `inish` vanished and a truncated value nearly went to Save.
cause: The page's buttons do not react to a synthetic JS click; only a trusted mouse click (`page.mouse.click` at coordinates) opens the modal. The modal's field re-renders after the selection is replaced, so the first keydowns reach a node that no longer exists. Both races are invisible without reading the value back.
rule: In a logged-in Chrome press UI elements with the real mouse at coordinates, not `.click()`. Before typing, clear the field and verify it is empty (Ctrl+A, Backspace, read the value), type with a delay and compare the value afterwards; press Save only on an exact match. A script that cannot prove it typed exactly what it meant must not save.

title: Markup sampled from page one of a list does not describe page two
symptom: A list parser returned 22 cards, five of them titled `last week`, `last week`, `last week`, `last week` and `Boosted` instead of titles. The regression was green and the production run showed no errors because it never reached page two.
cause: Fixtures were captured from the first page, where items are fresh: age reads `4 days ago` and the only badge is one known label. On page two older items have age spelled as words (`last week`, `last month`) and a different badge. Neither form was in the age or label patterns, so that line became the title. The cost is not just noise: the event key built from the title would diverge from the same event's key elsewhere, and one event would be reported twice.
rule: When sampling list markup, sample every page, not just the first: time changes not only the data but the words the site uses for it. Enumerate the age and badge forms explicitly and put a fixture from the farthest page into the regression.

title: A readiness check on the page scaffold returns before the data has loaded
symptom: A new read of list labels ran clean: 20 cards parsed, the `Viewed by client` label counted zero. Twenty minutes later the same page by hand showed the label present. No failure, no warning: a silently empty result that looks like 'nobody is looking'.
cause: The readiness condition checked the scaffold (the heading text), but cards and labels load through separate requests 1-3 s later; the read stopped at the first match. A 'two identical reads in a row' rule does not save you either: there can be a flat pause between the cards and the label, and both reads can fall into it (caught by a regression, not in production).
rule: Write the readiness condition on the data you came for, not on the scaffold around it; if the data may legitimately be absent, keep reading for a fixed few seconds and take the last non-empty read. Verify such code with a live run on the server: locally the page always looks ready.

title: An awk date filter `$0 >= "2026-..."` passes every line that starts with `[`
symptom: `awk '$0 >= "2026-08-28T08:00"' listener.log | grep -c "poll FAIL"` reported 443 failures 'in a day' (really 10 and 7), and a 'funnel since the fix' turned out to be the whole history; half an hour went into a non-existent outage.
cause: Log lines start with `[`, and `[` (0x5B) is greater than any digit in ASCII, so `$0 >= "2026-..."` is true for every line; the output looked plausible (large but not absurd numbers).
rule: Compare the date with the same prefix as the line (`substr($0,1,len) >= "[2026-08-28T08:00"`), and before raising any alarm check on the first printed line that its timestamp is at or after the boundary; if 'count for the period' equals 'count for all time', the filter is not working.

title: HTTP/3 over filtered UDP costs ~30 s per request; Chrome never marks QUIC broken
symptom: Poll hangs followed one pattern: first request reads, the second hangs 60 s (`Navigation timeout`), context reset, one request lost: 40 of 93 polls one day, 50 of 85 the next. A recovered tab stuck for 4.5 minutes on `Waiting for <site> to respond`. Evidence (rendered page, 'renderer did not answer in 5 s', `curl` 403 in 1-2 s, Chrome at 10-20% CPU) pointed nowhere for two days.
cause: Resource Timing of the recovered tab: the document's `requestStart - fetchStart` was 270 s, i.e. the request sat in Chrome's queue; static assets over `h3`: p50 27.9 s, p90 31 s at a 1.5 KB median, the same over `h2`: p50 2.4 s. Outbound UDP is filtered from this address, yet the profile's `Network Persistent State` had alt-svc `h3` for every host and an empty `broken_alternative_services`: Chrome kept retrying QUIC. A silent renderer and a request waiting on a stalled connection look identical from outside.
rule: For a hung navigation ask about the protocol and timings first (`performance.getEntriesByType('navigation'|'resource')`: `nextHopProtocol`, `requestStart - fetchStart`, `responseStart`), not just whether the renderer is alive. Where UDP is filtered, disable QUIC explicitly (`--disable-quic`) instead of trusting the broken-alt-svc logic. Verify afterwards: no `h3` in timings, static p90 under 0.2 s, polls 9/9 in 60-90 s.

title: A heartbeat's retry window must cover the gap to the next ping
symptom: The external health check reported DOWN while the daemon was fully alive (polls 9/9, `NRestarts=0`): the ping after one poll hit a 10 s timeout twice, and the next chance came only after the next poll 16 minutes later. Fourth such case in six days.
cause: Window arithmetic: the check expects a ping every 20 min plus 10 min grace = 30 min; pings come every 15-17 min, so one missed ping is always an alarm. The single retry after 5 s covered a hiccup of up to 15 s; the real one lasted 25 s or more. The alarm measured one 25-second stretch of network, not the daemon.
rule: Make the heartbeat retry window at least the interval between pings (here up to 10 attempts one minute apart); log the outcome of every ping and a success-after-retry as its own line, otherwise stutters are invisible and an empty grep lies. Before wiring any external check compute (period + grace) - signal interval = how many seconds of hiccup it forgives.

title: A fully covered Chrome window silently drops CDP input (visibilityState hidden)
symptom: Two runs hung on human-like mouse clicks; a third typed a title and tags into nothing (field values unchanged, no errors). `document.visibilityState === 'hidden'` with `windowState: normal`: another application's window was covering Chrome.
cause: Windows occlusion tracking: a fully covered Chrome moves the renderer to the background and does not deliver synthetic input (the mouse waits for an ack forever, keys are lost). Earlier successful edits ran while the window was visible.
rule: Before any CDP input check `document.visibilityState === 'visible'`; launch channel Chromes with `--disable-backgrounding-occluded-windows --disable-renderer-backgrounding --disable-background-timer-throttling --disable-features=CalculateNativeWinOcclusion`; an already running Chrome is cured only by a restart. Put every script step under a timeout (`Promise.race`) with a log file so a hang is visible instead of a bare `Terminated`.

title: A secret removed from a file still lives in git history and in daily bundles
symptom: A secret answer was removed from a tracked file by an audit, but `git grep` over `rev-list --all` still found it in 171 versions of the file; the same commits sat in daily `*.bundle` backups posted to a chat.
cause: Deleting a line is a new commit on top of the old ones; history, the remote and the bundles keep every previous version. 'Removed from the file' is not 'removed from the project's memory'.
rule: A secret that reached the repo is purged by rewriting history: `git filter-repo --replace-text` (locally, `pip install --user --break-system-packages git-filter-repo`), `git push --force`, and on the server `git fetch && git reset --hard origin/master && git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc --prune=now` with the sync timer stopped; old bundles are deleted by a human. Commit hashes after the first affected one change, so older hash references become historical. Cheapest of all: never write the secret; if you did, purge it in the same session while it is one commit deep.

title: React inline fields save only on Enter after validate(); fill() skips state
symptom: A profile title 'saved' (the field went readonly) but came back old after reload; `fill` into a textarea put 542 characters into the DOM while the counter still said `Minimum 150 characters`; skill suggestions never appeared on programmatic input.
cause: (1) The inline fields send nothing on blur, Tab or `element.blur()`; the save request goes only on Enter and only if the component's `validate(text)` returns `null`, and the error is visible only as an `isError` flag in React props (the tagline allowed letters, digits, spaces and `, : ' ! ?`; dot, dash, `&`, `+`, `/` and brackets were rejected). (2) `fill` writes the DOM value past React state; the cure is the native `value` setter plus `dispatchEvent(new Event('input',{bubbles:true}))`. (3) The typeahead reacts only to real keystrokes; suggestions render as radio labels.
rule: For such inline fields: run the text through the component's `validate` from its props first (fiber then `memoizedProps.validate`), set the value via the native setter plus an `input` event, press a real Enter, then always reload and re-read the value: 'the field closed' is not 'it saved'.

title: Agent Bash shell lacks Windows interop dirs in PATH: powershell.exe not found
symptom: The bridge bring-up script printed `powershell.exe: command not found` and then ten `NOT reachable` attempts; Chrome never started and no UAC prompt appeared.
cause: The tool's Bash shell has a PATH without the Windows directories (interop works, but `/mnt/c/Windows/System32/...` is not on PATH).
rule: Before bridge scripts run `export PATH="$PATH:/mnt/c/Windows/System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0:/mnt/c/Windows/System32"`; the signature of this failure is a `command not found` line before the UAC line.

title: A silent slice(0, N) on the way to a model reads as 'nothing more was written'
symptom: 6 of 33 descriptions in a day reached the model at exactly 3000 characters, and a job was skipped with 'truncated technical overview without a list of what is needed': the list was beyond the cut.
cause: The parser cut `summary` at 3000 characters silently; the prompt received the length and the source but not the fact of truncation, so the model read the cut as 'the client did not describe the task'. The mirror case (short is not unread) had been fixed earlier without looking at the other end of the distribution.
rule: Any `slice(0, N)` on the way to a model must (a) set the limit from the distribution with headroom, (b) leave a marker in the text (`[truncated at N of M characters]`), (c) reach the prompt as a fact. When fixing one end of a threshold, check the other end.

title: `claude -p` has tools on by default; a 'no tools needed' prompt can read .env
symptom: The wrapper called `claude -p --output-format json --json-schema ...` without `--tools ""`; `cwd` was `$HOME`, where `.env` (bot token, IMAP password), `~/.claude/.credentials.json` and a Chrome profile with a live session were readable. The model read untrusted text about 30 times a day, and the prompts never said 'the job text is data, not instructions'.
cause: 'Tools are not needed' was read as 'there are none'. The token's blast radius had been narrowed for exactly this injection surface, but the model's own tools were left alone because the prompt did not ask for them.
rule: For any headless model call set the tool list explicitly (`--tools ""`, available in CLI 2.1.x; structured output still works) and declare untrusted text in the prompt as data. Test by refusal: a prompt asking to read `~/.env` must return a refusal, not the contents.

title: Xvfb without a window manager cannot raise a window; rehearse the action
symptom: The fallback path 'a human clicks a verification on the server over noVNC' was rehearsed in the morning and still broken in the afternoon: the needed window could not be brought to the front.
cause: The rehearsal covered the channel (tunnel, picture, mouse movement), not the whole action. On display `:99` there was no window manager: windows cannot be switched, there is no active window, only whatever was placed on top is visible. In a real failure the needed window would be underneath.
rule: A rehearsal passes only when the final action is performed under the same conditions as the failure (same window, same order, same person). 'Access exists' is not 'it can be done'. Fix: a window-manager unit on the server.

title: A successful navigation is not a live page: explicit timeout on every evaluate
symptom: The daemon was `active`, six minutes without a log line, then a vague `Runtime.callFunctionOn timed out`. The human never learned that an interstitial page was sitting on screen, which is exactly what the signal was written for.
cause: On the interstitial page the renderer does not respond to `evaluate` at all. The code waited for puppeteer's default `protocolTimeout` of 180 s, and the first call swallowed the timeout as 'empty text' and moved on. The 'is this an interstitial?' check only lived in the navigation-failure branch, and the navigation had succeeded.
rule: Every call into another process gets its own explicit deadline, shorter than any default. Treat silence from the other process as the worst known cause and alert the human, instead of recording an empty result and moving on.

title: A screenshot sent as evidence must prove it was taken now
symptom: An alert went out with an image captioned 'what is on screen' that had nothing to do with what was on screen.
cause: The screenshot was written to the same file every time, and on a wedged renderer `screenshot` did not return within the allotted 10 s. The race moved on, the path still went into the error text, and the previous frame was sent.
rule: An artifact sent as proof must carry a freshness signal (it was captured right now). If it could not be captured, say so in words; never send 'the latest available' in place of the current one.

title: When a browser daemon goes silent, ask Chrome (`/json/list`), not the log
symptom: The cause of hangs was searched in logs for a day and not found: the log held a single line, `timeout`.
cause: The log is written only after a call returns; a hung call writes nothing. The state lived elsewhere: in Chrome itself.
rule: If a daemon is silent, look first at the state of what it controls: `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/list` showed the tab URL within a second. And leave evidence for yourself: a screenshot, the URL and the renderer's answer on every timeout.

title: Node 20 abandons connects after 250 ms (Happy Eyeballs); a slow link looks dead
symptom: An external health check went DOWN; the Telegram poller logged `poll FAIL fetch failed` 106 times over 38 minutes; the heartbeat failed twice. From the same machine `curl` reached both hosts, `dig` resolved them, SSH did not blink, and `fetch` from the same Node to a CDN-fronted site answered 403 in 462 ms.
cause: Node 20 enables Happy Eyeballs by default with `autoSelectFamilyAttemptTimeout = 250 ms`: an attempt is killed after a quarter second and the next address is tried, and the started one is not kept. The server has no global IPv6 (only `fe80::`), so AAAA addresses fail instantly, and the real TCP connect that day took 0.27-1.29 s. The error arrived after exactly 250 ms times the number of IPv4 addresses (255 ms for one address, 1112 ms for four). `curl` does not abandon a started attempt, so it worked.
rule: Test 'the network is down' with the same client that failed, not with `ping` or `curl`: identical results mean network, different results mean client. Raise the threshold explicitly for a Node daemon on a slow link (`net.setDefaultAutoSelectFamilyAttemptTimeout`, here 5 s); `--dns-result-order=ipv4first` does not help (same ETIMEDOUT, tested).

title: Treating partial success as success silences the external watchdog
symptom: Two polls in a row read only one query out of ten (nine hung for 60 s each), and the monitor reported a normal `poll done`, pinged the external watchdog and said nothing in the chat. The 'three polls without results' signal did not fire: it counts polls with zero, and here there was one success.
cause: `okSearches` was used as a boolean 'something was read'. The external check would show 'monitor alive' while it was 90% blind: the pipeline wrote itself an alibi.
rule: Health is a ratio, not a fact: a pass counts as healthy only if at least half of the queries were read. Ping the external watchdog only on a healthy pass; log an incomplete one separately and report a streak with numbers. More generally: for any success/failure aggregate, ask what it looks like at 10% success.

title: A check that cannot answer 'no' is a constant: count a predicate's answers
symptom: A `jobAlive` function answered 'alive' for five days on every question, closed jobs included. No error in the logs: the 'closed by client' rule simply never fired.
cause: Liveness was read as `fetch('https://.../jobs/~id/')` from an open tab, judged by the words `no longer available` in the response. The site answered a programmatic request with a 403 interstitial that never contains those words, so a negative answer was physically unreachable: the function could only return `true` or throw.
rule: Ask of any predicate not 'does it work' but 'what does its negative answer look like and have we ever seen one'. If the logs contain no `false`, the check is considered broken until shown otherwise on a deliberately broken case. In log reviews count the distribution of each predicate's answers, and keep a fixture for the 'no' branch (the interstitial text and a closed-item text).

title: Disconnecting from Chrome does not remove the browser contexts a process created
symptom: Chrome on the server accumulated 12 pages, 10 iframes and 30 workers, using 2.7 GB of 3.9 GB. Nine of the pages were copies of search results and item pages nobody touched.
cause: On every process start the monitor creates its own incognito context (`browser.createBrowserContext()`) and on exit only disconnects. The context with all its tabs stays in Chrome forever: every daemon restart adds one live page that keeps eating memory. Cleanup existed only for item tabs in the default context.
rule: Disconnect is not cleanup. Whatever a process created inside a long-lived foreign application (context, tab, temporary profile) it must remove either on exit or on the next start; the latter is more reliable because it survives a crash. Verify live, not by reading code: count objects in the application before and after a restart. Result here: 12 pages to 2, 2707 MB to 1128 MB.

title: A page returned on timeout with partial content looks like an empty page
symptom: Five of 72 alerts ended in a model refusal with 'the description breaks off mid-sentence' or 'generic phrases without a single fact'. All five had an empty full description and an unread secondary block: the page simply had not finished loading.
cause: The fetch waited up to 30 s for text and on timeout returned whatever had rendered, without an error. The parser then honestly returned empty fields, and the drafter fell back to the card summary from the listing, which is truncated to 300 characters on write. The model got a fragment without knowing it was one.
rule: Distinguish 'read and empty' from 'not read': a read of an external page needs a completeness flag, and no decision is made on incomplete data (either re-read or tell the model explicitly that the description is incomplete). Truncation when writing a log (300 chars) is not a storage detail but a ceiling on decision quality when someone decides from that log.

title: Retry idempotent steps by default; clean up on every exit path, exit(1) too
symptom: A fresh item in the best band dropped out of the funnel entirely: `claude FAIL error_max_structured_output_retries`. No retry with the same model, no fallback to the next, and the form tab opened for a read stayed in Chrome.
cause: Fallback was triggered only when the error text matched `limit|overloaded|429|rate.?limit|credit|quota`. A new kind of error ('the model could not fit the schema in N tries') missed the list and was treated as fatal. On that branch the script exited via `process.exit(1)`, bypassing `closeForm()`.
rule: For an idempotent step (a request without side effects) retry by default: at least one retry on any failure, with a whitelist for errors that are pointless to retry. Every emergency exit path gets the same cleanup as the normal one: if a function opened a tab, all exits close it, including `exit(1)`.

title: A command-line flag does not survive into deferred work sent by another process
symptom: A test marker was added as the first line of `--test-alert` output. But the test email also creates a reminder, and reminders 45 and 180 minutes later are sent by the inbox daemon, a separate process started without flags: only the first message would carry the marker, the next two would look real.
cause: The mode lived in `process.argv`, i.e. in the memory of one run, while the event outlived that run: it was written to `state/pending/<key>.json` and became another process's work. Whatever outlives its process loses the mode at the boundary.
rule: If an action leaves a record from which someone else will later send a message, the mode marker goes into that record (`test: true`), not only into the current output. Check by asking: who sends the next message about this event, and do they know it is a test?

title: ImapFlow uidValidity is a BigInt; JSON.stringify throws, systemd still 'active'
symptom: The inbox daemon was deployed, the unit was `active`, 30 selftest checks were green on both machines. The daemon parsed no mail: it was crash-looping a fraction of a second after opening the mailbox, and `systemctl is-active` kept answering `active` because the process came up between crashes.
cause: ImapFlow returns `mailbox.uidValidity` as a BigInt, and `JSON.stringify` throws `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt`. Saving state is the first thing the daemon does on a new mailbox. The fixtures could not contain that value: they were hand-written, and the type came from the library. Second layer: `active` in systemd means the process is alive, not that the work is being done.
rule: Convert everything that enters state from an external library to your own type at the boundary (`Number(...)`, `String(...)`). After deployment look at the daemon's own log and an artifact of its work (state file, ledger line, chat message), not the unit status: the first live run is a separate acceptance step.

title: Alert extremes: firing every 30 s under Restart=always, or exactly once
symptom: Found by reading the code before hand-off. With `Restart=always`, a missing password in `.env` made the daemon post 'did not start' and exit: it would post that every 30 seconds forever. The opposite extreme in the same file: with IMAP dead the alert went out on the third failure and never again, and the daily canary went quiet together with IMAP, so a broken daemon would look like 'all quiet'.
cause: Alerts were written case by case and none answered 'what will the human see if the cause persists for a week'. A hammering alert gets muted together with the channel; a single one gets lost in the feed.
rule: Give every alert two numbers: a frequency cap (a marker file with a timestamp, at most once per N hours) and a repeat period while the cause persists. Separately check that the self-check does not fall silent with the alert: if the canary lives inside the broken loop, silence proves nothing.

title: An irreversible action in a foreign UI goes last and is verified by outcome
symptom: Exploring a bidding widget: a number typed into the field means nothing until `Set bid` is pressed (`Bid: 0` with `18` in the field). After pressing, the bid becomes part of the form and cannot be taken back: clearing the field and pressing again does not reset it.
cause: In a foreign interface state lives elsewhere than where you type: the field is a draft, the commit is a separate event, and undo may not exist. The habit 'set it, check, redo if needed' comes from your own code where rollback is free.
rule: Put an action that cannot be undone last in the chain, after every check that could cancel it, and verify by the observable outcome (what the form shows, what the submit button says), not by what you typed. Outcome differs from intent means do not submit at all.

title: A stage that silently drops candidates makes any audit impossible
symptom: Asked 'did we wrongly skip anything overnight', the logs could not answer: 8 of 15 new items vanished before the drafter without a single line. Each cause had to be reconstructed by re-running the filter function over the saved JSONL.
cause: The monitor had `const why = cheapFilter(j); if (why) continue;`: decision made, nothing recorded. Every other stage logged its reason; the cheapest and most frequent one did not, precisely because it looked like 'just a filter'.
rule: Every stage that rejects a candidate must leave a line 'what was rejected and why', including the cheapest and most obvious. Test while writing: could I answer next week why a specific item did not reach the end without running anything? If the answer is 'I would re-run the code over the data', the record does not exist.

title: Scattered network errors were one filtered UDP/53 uplink; ping proves nothing
symptom: In one day: git sync failed with `Temporary failure in name resolution`, the external watchdog reported the monitor DOWN, two browser searches failed with `ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED`. `ping` to 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, the hoster's resolver and the gateway showed 0% loss and flat RTT.
cause: The first DNS uplink in `netplan` was 8.8.8.8, and outbound UDP/53 is filtered from this network: `dig @8.8.8.8` answered 3 of 20, `@1.1.1.1` 5 of 20, the datacenter's local resolver 19 of 20, while `dig +tcp` to both public ones was 5/5. `systemd-resolved` preferred the first server and waited for a timeout on each miss. ICMP is answered by the router/resolver itself and says nothing about UDP packets to port 53.
rule: When 'random' network errors appear across several daemons on one machine, look for the shared lower layer (resolver, MTU, uplink) rather than fixing each daemon. Measure DNS by resolving through each uplink separately (`dig @server`, a series of 20), not by ping, and do it on day one of a rented machine: the hoster's default may be nearly non-functional. Public resolvers are not a universal answer; the datacenter's or provider's resolver is often the only working one.

title: An alert without a threshold and an all-clear wakes a human on every hiccup
symptom: The sync job posted 'did not push history' after one failed run (two attempts within 70 s). The next run 4 minutes later succeeded, cleared its internal alert stamp and said nothing: the human had to go to the server to find out whether sync was still down.
cause: The job knew one state: 'broke, report'. No threshold, so a one-minute stutter equalled a prolonged outage; no recovery notice because at writing time only the failure seemed to matter.
rule: An automatic alert needs three things: a threshold (N consecutive failures, not the first), an all-clear through the same channel when the job recovers, and a consecutive-failure counter reset by success. A retry inside one run does not count as a threshold: for the network it is the same instant. The same pattern applied to the heartbeat (a second ping after 5 s before going silent).

title: Type=oneshot defaults to TimeoutStartSec=infinity; a hung run stops the timer
symptom: A sync service run started while DNS was down sat in `activating` for over two minutes. While the service is active the timer schedules nothing, so memory sync stood still with no alert: the script never reached its alert branch.
cause: For `Type=oneshot` the default `TimeoutStartSec` is `infinity`, and `ssh` without `ConnectTimeout` waits for the TCP timeout for minutes. The script had a 'broke' branch but no 'hung' branch, although for a periodic job hanging is worse than failing: a failure shows in the log and unit status, a hang looks like silence.
rule: Bound a periodic job's time in two places: in the command itself (`ConnectTimeout`/`ServerAliveInterval` for ssh, `--max-time` for curl) and in the unit (`TimeoutStartSec` below the timer period times a small factor). Test not only 'what if it fails' but 'what if it never answers'.

title: systemd After= orders startup; it does not wait for the neighbour's readiness
symptom: After every reboot the monitor's first poll failed entirely with eight `Failed to fetch browser webSocket URL`, and the next poll 15 minutes later worked. The unit honestly had `After=chrome.service` and `Wants=`.
cause: `After=` guarantees only launch order. Chrome is `Type=simple`, so systemd considers it started at `exec`, while the CDP port opens 2-3 seconds later. The monitor landed in that gap, and its self-healing made it worse by restarting a Chrome that had not come up yet.
rule: When a daemon depends on a neighbour's readiness (open port, socket, health endpoint) rather than its launch, add an explicit wait: `ExecStartPre` polling the endpoint, time-bounded, prefixed with `-` so an unavailable neighbour does not turn into a daemon that never starts. `After=`/`Wants=` are not enough; `Type=notify` on the neighbour is better but not always possible with a foreign binary. Fix the cause in the unit rather than compensating in the production loop (retrying the poll would have turned the failure alert into spam).

title: A GitHub deploy key added via the API dies with the token that created it
symptom: Access was narrowed (deploy keys instead of an account token), tested by refusal and success, and the owner was asked to revoke the token. A minute after revocation the server reported it could not sync; `ssh` with the key answered `Permission denied (publickey)`: revoking the classic token removed both deploy keys, because they had been added through the API with that token.
cause: Acceptance checked the radius of the new access (where the key reaches and where it does not) and never its dependence on the old secret. The order was the reverse of the safe one: revoke first, then learn that the new path hung on the revoked one.
rule: When replacing access, first make sure the new path was not created by the secret being revoked and will survive its revocation (for GitHub: add deploy keys by hand in the repository's Settings, Deploy keys, not via the API with a token; a key added in the UI belongs to the owner). Consider access replaced only after the old secret is revoked and the new path is re-tested. Also check `~/.ssh/config` and `ssh -T git@github.com` before generating yet another key.

title: Judge a secret by what it opens when stolen, not by where it is stored
symptom: The setup was called safe by the formal test 'the token is only in `.env`, mode 600, not in git, not in backups', all true. The question 'what does this token open?' showed a classic token with `repo, workflow` scopes opening every repository of the account, including an unrelated private one, on a rented VPS where a headless model reads untrusted text every 15 minutes.
cause: 'Secrets only in `.env`' is a rule about leakage, not about privileges. It silently assumes the secret has the right scope, and on a machine running automation over untrusted input that assumption is the hole. The token was also reused: issued months earlier for publishing demos, then handed to the sync job because it was at hand.
rule: For any secret on an automated machine ask not 'where is it' but 'what can be done with it if read', and trim it to exactly what is needed. For git that is a per-repository deploy key, not an account token: it does not open the API at all. Test the narrowing by refusal (try reaching a neighbouring repository), not only by success. A secret that has been on a rented machine counts as compromised: revoke, do not migrate.

title: git pull --rebase needs a committer identity; -c on commit alone is not enough
symptom: A new two-way sync was tested in both directions and ran green three times, then posted a real alert 'could not reconcile history' twice. The log only said `pull FAIL`. The first explanation (a manual `git fetch` colliding with the timer's `pull`) was plausible by timing and wrong.
cause: `git pull --rebase` rewrites the server's own commits, which needs a committer identity, and the repository had none: the script passed `-c user.name/user.email` only to `commit`. Hence `fatal: empty ident name` and an aborted rebase. The hole hid until the first simultaneous divergence: while only one side had new commits, pull was a fast-forward with nothing to rewrite.
rule: Test a two-way exchange on simultaneous divergence (one commit on each side, then see who rebases whom), not one direction at a time. Settings passed with `-c` apply to that command only: operations that rewrite commits (`rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `commit --amend`) need the identity separately, so put it in the repository config and duplicate it in the script. Log stderr immediately, otherwise diagnoses are built on timing coincidences.

title: An automatic git sync must roll back on any failure and shout
symptom: The first version of the sync script did `git pull --rebase || exit 1`. On a conflict (both machines appended the same ledger) the server would stay in an unfinished rebase: files with conflict markers, `.git/rebase-merge` on disk, and that tree is read by live daemons.
cause: A human failure scenario was assumed for an automatic operation: a human would see the conflict and sort it out. A daemon has no spectator; it carries any unfinished state into the next cycle, and the failure is silent because the error went to a log nobody reads.
rule: Every automatic operation that changes a working tree needs an explicit return to the initial state on any failure (`git rebase --abort`, transaction rollback, lock release) and a voice in a live channel with an anti-spam marker. Verify by a controlled failure, not by reasoning: break the remote address, trigger the service, confirm the tree is clean, the alert arrived and the next run is green again.

title: Whoever opens a side resource closes it, on every exit path including returns
symptom: After 13 hours on the server, the logged-in Chrome held two open form tabs, exactly as many as items the model had skipped. No errors in the logs and no `tabs closed` lines at all.
cause: The drafter opens the form tab for a read before the model's decision, and only the listener closed it, on the draft's terminal status. A skipped item has no draft and never reaches the listener, so the `decision !== 'draft'` branch returned past any cleanup. Classic asymmetry: cleanup on the success path, three early exits without it.
rule: If a function opens a side resource (tab, context, file, lock) for an intermediate read, the release is written next to the open and covers all exits, including early returns on refusal. Do not rely on the next component in the chain: it runs only on some paths. Cheap check: `curl -s http://<cdp>/json/list` and count pages; more than expected means a path without cleanup.

title: A top-N error summary must apply N to normalized kinds, not raw lines
symptom: The morning summary said 'errors in logs: 90' and listed five, all the same network stutter of the chat poller. Real events of the same night (`search FAIL: net::ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED`, a failed heartbeat ping) did not make it into the message.
cause: The summary took `errs.slice(0, 5)`, the first five lines in file order. One class repeated dozens of times fills the whole display, and the noisier the channel, the more reliably the rare event hides.
rule: Apply N to kinds, not lines: normalize the message (numbers to `N`), group, show each kind with its multiplicity (`11x poll FAIL fetch failed`). The noisy class takes one line and the rare event is always visible. Keep the total line count next to it: it reports the health of the link.

title: A migration is not done while the old machine can resurrect daemons at login
symptom: After moving the pipeline to the server, the laptop daemons were stopped and no processes remained. A review found a live `.vbs` in the Windows Startup folder: at the next login the laptop would have started a second copy of the pipeline.
cause: Processes were killed, not the mechanism that starts them. Autostart is a separate entity that survives stopping daemons and powering off, and is visible only in its own place (Startup folder, scheduler, systemd `enabled`, cron).
rule: The last step of any migration is to disarm autostart on the old machine, checked in the old platform's own terms (Windows: `Get-ChildItem "$env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"` and `Get-ScheduledTask`). Disable by renaming (`.disabled-<date>`) rather than deleting, since returning to the old machine is also the rollback plan. The cost of skipping it is concrete: two pollers fighting over the same API (409) and two auto-submitters acting twice on one item.

title: A health indicator bound to the old supervisor's PID file lies under systemd
symptom: The first `/status` after the migration answered 'monitor: STOPPED' although the monitor was running and the same line said 'last poll: 11 min ago'.
cause: Liveness was derived from `state/monitor.pid`, written by the supervisor loop of the old `run.sh`. Under systemd there is no PID file, so the check silently fell into STOPPED. The same root could give the opposite error: 'running' from a stale PID file.
rule: Bind health indicators to a fact, not to an artifact of one supervisor: a live process or the freshness of the last work result. When the launch method changes (setsid to systemd, systemd to a container), run every control command first and compare its answer with reality; they break silently because nothing formally fails.

title: systemd Requires= stops dependents with the dependency and never restarts them
symptom: The monitor and the chat listener were `inactive` after Chrome had been stopped for 5 seconds to test the bridge's self-healing. Chrome came back, the daemons did not; logs empty, units not `failed`, restart counter 0: it looked like a normal stop while the channel was dead.
cause: The units had `Requires=chrome.service`, a hard two-way binding: stopping Chrome stops the dependents, and restarting it does not bring them back. The monitor does not need that binding at all: it survives a missing browser (20 s timeout) and re-launches the bridge itself.
rule: Use hard `Requires=` only where the process physically cannot start without the dependency (Chrome without Xvfb). Everywhere else `Wants=` plus `After=`: launch order is kept, cascade failure is not. Add `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` in `[Unit]`, otherwise after a series of crashes systemd stops restarting the daemon and it silently stays down. Mandatory one-command test: stop the dependency and confirm the daemon stays `active`.

title: rsync of code from the laptop overwrites the server's machine-specific config
